commit.message:
the demo script would have overwritten the domain 60 seconds before recording

Step 2 said to run scripts/tunnel-keeper.sh. That was right yesterday and is
now the worst instruction in the repository: the keeper republishes a cloudflare
quick-tunnel hostname whenever the chain disagrees with what it is serving, so
following the script would have replaced the reserved domain minutes before the
take, silently, and the failure would have arrived mid-demo as a machine nobody
could reach.

The setup is the reserved domain and `npm run rotate` now, and the keeper itself
refuses to start when the published hostname is not a quick tunnel — KEEPER_FORCE=1
if you really mean it. A guard in the script beats a warning in a document,
because the document is what gets skimmed at 2am.

The desk also stops leaving people staring at a dead panel: when no signed
outcome comes back it now says to press the button again and why that works —
a repeat is answered from the enclave's memory in seconds, because the auction
is already cleared. That is the same fix the loop got, in the place a human
actually stands.

And two checks for the affordances a cleared auction must NOT offer: sealing a
bid and requesting another clearing both revert AlreadyCleared, so showing
either is offering a transaction that can only fail, paid for.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

the machine is on a reserved domain now, not a quick tunnel

nonmultiplicative-florida-macromolecular.ngrok-free.dev, published on-chain and
answering. It is the last operational caveat the submission carried, and it is
the one Flare states as a rule in the pinned message: data providers push to the
URL on-chain, so a hostname that changes leaves a machine unreachable and stuck.

Two things had to be fixed to get there. The agent was 3.3.1 and the account
requires 3.20.0 — the failure reads `authentication failed`, which sends you
looking at the token. And post-build.sh does NOT update the hostname of a
machine that is already registered; it re-attests the one on record. So the
availability check went to the tunnel we had just abandoned, came back 404, and
reported a failed registration while everything local was healthy. The script
publishes the hostname first now, and dies if it cannot.

The honest-scope note says what is true today: a reserved domain, and still a
tunnel to a machine under a desk rather than hosted infrastructure.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

the keeper would have overwritten the static domain within a minute

tunnel-register-ngrok.sh writes a permanent hostname on-chain, and
tunnel-keeper.sh republishes a cloudflare quick-tunnel URL every 60 seconds
whenever the chain disagrees with what it is serving. Run one while the other
is alive and the static domain lasts under a minute — with no error anywhere,
because both are doing exactly what they were told. The symptom would arrive
much later, as a machine that went unreachable for no visible reason.

It refuses to start now if a keeper is running, and says which two processes to
stop. That is a footgun with the deadline on the other side of it: the switch to
a static domain is the last operational item before the video.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

say what the enclave actually does with the amounts it holds

The solvency screen has been the strongest confidential-compute argument in this
codebase and the submission called it future work, because it was written after
the document and only ran in the facade. Now that it is live in the enclave that
settles, it is a claim with evidence behind it.

The point is not that a screen exists — a contract could refuse an unfunded
winner too, after the fact and after wasting the deadline. It is WHERE it runs:
only the enclave can ask "could this bidder pay what they would owe" without
answering the other question, which is what they bid. The maker learns nothing.
The bidder who is dropped learns nothing. Everyone else sees the same winner and
second price they would have seen anyway.

The trust section says the matching thing: what the enclave sees is bounded and
stated — it clears, it screens, it forgets, including the winner's own bid,
which Vickrey never reveals and which an enclave that kept it could only leak.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

clearing the same auction twice is an answer, not an error

The intermittency that cost three runs today was not the network. One
requestClearing is delivered to the enclave more than once — the data providers
push it under a `threshold` tag and an `end` tag, and the main and backup queues
can both carry it — and only the threshold result carries the four-word ABI
outcome relayClearing can settle. `end` carries an 1887-byte consensus envelope
that is signed, valid, and useless for settling.

processClearAuction returned ErrAlreadyClosed for every delivery after the
first. So whichever arrived first won, and when that was `end`, the settleable
result came back as status 0 and the auction could not be settled at all. From
the outside it looked like "no signed outcome came back in time", which reads as
a slow chain and is why it survived this long. The proxy log said it plainly the
whole time:

  received failed result … tag threshold … log: error: auction: already cleared

A repeat now returns the stored outcome with status 1. Nothing leaks: after a
clearing the winner and the price are public by construction, and the losing
amounts were already zeroed by the run that did the work. It cannot re-run the
auction either — the openings are gone, so this is an answer from memory.

TestClearTwiceRejected asserted the bug, so it is now
TestClearTwiceReturnsTheSameOutcome: same bytes both times, and decoding the
repeat matches the stored outcome.

Proven on Coston2: rebuilt, recreated, rotated, and RFQ 13 settled on the FIRST
attempt — every previous run after a recreate needed two or three. The proxy now
logs the same instruction answered twice, threshold then end, both status 1.

Also scripts/rotate.mjs (npm run rotate): register, point the contract at it,
retire the machine it replaced, update the documents, then check all of it from
the chain. Each step skipped when the chain already says it is done. The two
steps people forget are the two that fail silently.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

the solvency screen was wired into the process nobody deploys

It is in the submission, it has seven tests, and `internal/extension` implements
it properly — and the only place that ever switched it on was cmd/dev, the local
facade. The enclave in the container, the one that actually clears auctions and
signs outcomes people settle against, ran with the screen off. Everything about
the feature was true except where it happened.

extension.New reads BUTA_FUNDS_RPC now, so both entry points get it from the same
place, and the dev-only copy is gone. The spender comes from INSTRUCTION_SENDER
when BUTA_INSTRUCTION_SENDER is unset — that is the name config/extension.env
uses, so docker-compose feeds the container the address that was deployed and it
cannot drift from the contract. The compose override turns it on for Coston2 and
says why: a bidder who cannot pay wins, relayClearing reverts on the
transferFrom, the auction dies and the runner-up who could have paid gets
nothing. Bidding costs nothing, so that is an attack on the maker.

Proved rather than assumed: enclave recreated with the screen on, re-registered,
rotated, and RFQ 10 settled on Coston2. The test asserts New() comes up with a
screen when the environment says so — the previous tests all built the extension
through a helper that could never have caught this.

Also scripts/sync-machine-address.mjs, because the machine address in the two
submission documents has now been wrong four times in one day. It derives the
address from the key the proxy is serving, refuses to write it unless the chain
says PRODUCTION, and --check fails when they disagree.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

the landing was still pointing at the first contract

Two links and a short label, both to 0x20d9CcAA — the deployment before the one
that was replaced today. A judge clicking through from the masthead landed on a
contract with no auctions on it.

Nothing caught it because nothing was looking there. The sweep after the
redeploy covered .md, .ts, .tsx, .mjs and .json; the landing is .html. The DOM
checks never asserted the address, and the pixel baselines could not: a mono
address is small enough that changing it moves less than the 0.2% tolerance.

qa/flows-landing.mjs now asks the diamond which contract is bound to the
extension and requires every explorer link on the page to be that one, plus the
short form to end in the same four characters. Reverted against the old address,
it fails both — which is the only reason to trust it.

Also verify:submission refuses an address stated with no link behind it: a
reader who cannot click it has to take it on trust, which is the one thing this
submission is not asking of anyone.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

the demo script is the run that passes, not the one that used to

DEMO_SCRIPT.md described the local facade: `go run ./cmd/dev`, a seeded book,
and a story that stopped at the clearing. The facade signs nothing, so the beat
that matters most now — the transaction that moves money — could not happen in
the demo it described, and the setup it listed no longer matches a deployment
that changed contract and extension today.

It is the live rail now, beat for beat as scripts/settle-from-browser.mjs just
drove it against 0xa03821AD…F74D: post on-chain, seal on-chain, request the
clearing, settle, then the explorer showing both transfers in one transaction.
The button labels are the real ones — "On-chain", "Seal on-chain instead",
"Request clearing on-chain", "Settle on-chain" — because a script that says
"click Post block" walks a nervous presenter straight onto the local rail, which
looks identical until nothing settles.

The two setup steps that are easy to skip are called out as such: setTeeAddress
after registering the machine, and retiring the previous one. Both fail silently
in the direction of a demo that just stops working on camera.

Also: HEADLESS=0 on the driver, so it can be the screen capture for the beats
you do not want to click twice. And the "Settled from the desk" row now cites
RFQ 8 on the live contract as well as the predecessor's.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

redeployed: extension 66009, and the receipts to say it works

The rotation fix cannot be shipped to an address that is already live, and the
registry has no call that repoints an extension at a new sender, so it took a
deploy and a fresh extension. 0xa03821AD…F74D, extension 66009, source-verified
on the explorer, machine 0x1608050E…3f62 registered and PRODUCTION.

Proven rather than asserted, in this order, all on Coston2:

  RFQ 1 settles                      0x5a5f867f…
  the container is replaced          the pinned enclave is now gone
  RFQ 2 cannot settle                which is the whole reason for the redeploy
  setTeeAddress rotates              0x0783b99b…
  RFQ 4 settles                      0x5ca111a5…
  RFQ 7 settles                      0x7d900f17…

Two runs in the middle died at "no signed outcome came back" and looked like a
slow network. They were not: the previous machine was still in the active set,
so getRandomTeeIds handed out either and half the instructions went to an
address nobody was listening on — with nothing reverting to say so. health.mjs
named it, retire-machine.mjs paused it, and the runs after that are clean.

verify:submission now checks the invariant that actually broke — that the
contract trusts the machine which is serving — and it is 14/14. The predecessor's
settlement receipts stay linked in SUBMISSION.md, marked as what they are.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

the contract address and extension id are read, not pinned

Every script kept its own copy of the extension id, and three kept their own
copy of the sender. Redeploying does not break that loudly — a stale sender is a
live contract that answers every call, about auctions nobody is looking at, and
a stale extension id reads the active set of an extension nobody serves. Both
report confidently.

onchain-status.mjs had been doing exactly that for two weeks: pinned to the very
first deployment, printing "teeAddress set → 0x1001…" — the deployer, on a
contract three deployments behind — while a different contract was live.

scripts/ext-config.mjs reads config/extension.env, which is the file the deploy
writes. The frontend takes the id from VITE_EXTENSION_ID, since it cannot read
that file, and asks the diamond for the sender rather than believing a constant.

onchain-loop.ts also waits six minutes for the signed outcome instead of two. The
result appears when enough data providers have voted, which is their schedule and
not ours; two minutes reported failures on runs where nothing was wrong.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

the enclave a deployment trusts has to be allowed to change

setTeeAddress could only ever run once. That is the wrong shape for what it
stores: a TEE identity is ephemeral on purpose — tee-node mints a signing key at
startup and never persists it, so the machine a contract is pinned to is
guaranteed to stop existing. The first replacement of the container left a live
contract with three settled auctions behind it and no fourth one possible, ever.
relayClearing reverted BadTeeSignature against a key nobody has.

It rotates now, and the registry is what makes that safe to allow: the argument
has to be a machine the diamond reports as PRODUCTION, which is a claim only the
availability check and the data providers can produce. An admin can pick among
attested machines; it cannot name an address and start signing.

Deliberately not the version that reads trustless — "accept any machine that is
PRODUCTION" at settle time. Every extension on the network registers into the
same registry, so that would let any other team's enclave sign a clearing that
moves this desk's money.

Three tests: the rotation, that the enclave it replaces stops settling the
moment it happens, and that a machine the diamond has not attested is refused
whether it is INITIALIZED or PAUSED.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

docs: the machine in the claims is the machine that is serving

tee-node mints a new key every start, so the machine address in SUBMISSION.md
and DORAHACKS_FORM.md named one that had been retired. The stack came back up
today as 0xB7b23B94…Ed7C, registered through the tunnel and PRODUCTION, with
every predecessor paused; verify:submission checks both of those, and it now
passes 11/11 again rather than failing the two rows about the machine.

The row itself said "the first machine is PAUSED", which read as a one-time
cleanup. It is not: it happens on every restart, by design, and the reason to
say so in the submission is that the alternative — leaving a dead machine in
the active set — fails silently. getRandomTeeIds keeps handing it out and
nothing reverts.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

build: the direct API key was in the public bundle

vite loads .env.local for PRODUCTION builds, not only dev. VITE_DIRECT_API_KEY
went in there when the desk needed it to read the real book, and it shipped
into dist — one `vercel --prod` from being public. It gates /direct on the
operator's proxy, so publishing it hands anyone the operator's read access.

Moved to .env.development.local, which `vite build` never reads, and the
assembler now greps the built bundle for it and fails the build.

That check was inert on its first attempt: it read process.env, and assemble.mjs
runs as its own process after vite, inheriting none of what vite loaded. It
found undefined, skipped every secret, and passed a build that did contain the
key. It reads the env files now, and putting the key back fails the build.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

the desk settles: tx 0xa07a748b, RFQ 11, driven through the UI

scripts/onchain-loop.ts has settled on Coston2 since 31 July. It shares its
libraries with the desk and builds its own arguments, so what it proved was the
contract and the enclave — never the product. Driving the actual pages found
four things, none of them visible from node:

The extension proxy sends no Access-Control-Allow-Origin header at all, so a
browser cannot reach it. /info, /direct and the signed-clearing poll were all
blocked before leaving the page. vite already proxies those paths in dev; the
absolute URL in .env.local was what bypassed it. Production needs the same
trick server-side — scripts/point-desk-at-machine.mjs writes Vercel rewrites,
and canReachExtension now asks /info instead of reading a build-time constant.

/direct is API-key gated. Without VITE_DIRECT_API_KEY the desk caught the 401
and quietly showed the DEMO book — and every on-chain button then took a demo
row's id straight to a transaction. One run sealed a real bid and requested a
real clearing on contract RFQ 5 while the operator was looking at demo row 5.
Row-scoped on-chain actions now refuse when the book is not real.

Settling lived only in the branch for an auction that had not cleared, so a
successful clearing removed the button that would settle it. Worse, the
signature lived in React state alone: reload and it was gone, and asking again
returns "auction: already cleared" — the enclave produces it exactly once. The
lot stayed escrowed with no route out. lib/clearings.ts writes it down.

And the tag is not the test. Only "threshold" carries the four-word ABI
outcome; "end" carries a 1887-byte {"voteSequence":…} envelope, signed and
status 1 and useless. Taking whichever answered first was a race the loop
happened to win twice. The desk decoded that leading `{` as an rfqId of
55695370586825141013624577… — caught by the mismatch guard, which refused.

Underneath all of it: USDT0 pointed at an address with no code. Every on-chain
block the desk ever posted was unsettleable from the moment it was posted.
A mintable TestToken now, the post form refuses an empty settlement token, and
sealing a bid approves the payment — winning means paying, and that approval
belongs at the promise, not at somebody else's reverting transaction.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

gas: every FAsset transfer had a ceiling it could hit

A reclaim reverted twice at gasUsed 116700 of a 118988 estimate. Nothing was
wrong with the call: FXRP is an FAsset, its transfer cost drifts between the
block the estimate is taken against and the block that executes, and the inner
ERC20 call only receives 63/64 of what is left. It runs out, returns false, and
the contract's own require(..., "lot refund failed") fires — which reads like a
refund bug and is really a gas ceiling.

The settlement that proved this system worked finished with 2% of its estimate
to spare. It succeeded by luck. Six write sites in the desk had the same
ceiling, and relayClearing makes TWO FAsset transfers, so it is the most
exposed of them — a starved settlement leaves the lot escrowed and the auction
open with both sides thinking they are done.

One wrapper, so there is one place to get it wrong. RFQ 3 settled with 51% to
spare instead of 2%, same script, no edits.

scripts/reclaim-stranded.mjs recovered the 26 FXRP that four retired
deployments were still holding — lots from auctions that never cleared, with no
route back except a raw transaction.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

the desk can now reach a clearing it can actually settle

Settle was wired to whatever the Clear button produced, and Clear goes down
the direct channel — which a production stack refuses outright
(BUTA_ALLOW_DIRECT_AUCTION is a demo switch, off there) and whose facade
signs nothing at all. So the desk could reach a clearing and then never
settle it, because relayClearing will not take an unsigned outcome. The
script proved the path; the product had no way to walk it.

"Request clearing on-chain" sends the transaction, pulls the instruction id
out of the diamond's log — topic 2, not topic 1, which is the extension id
and identical on every instruction — waits for the enclave to file a signed
result under it, decodes the abi-encoded outcome and hands it to Settle.

Renaming the button fails the check that it exists.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

the desk was talking to the first of four contracts

Every on-chain action — post, seal, reclaim, settle — and the Audit panel
pointed at a constant, and the constant was the FIRST deployment while
three later ones were live. A stale address does not throw: it reverts
every transaction against a contract nothing is bound to any more, and the
Audit panel cheerfully linked a judge to the wrong one.

Replacing the constant with a newer constant would only move the problem,
so the desk asks the diamond which contract is bound to extension 65642.
That is the authority, it is one eth_call, and it cannot go stale. The
constant survives as a last resort when the chain cannot be read.

Getting the check for it to bite took three attempts, all of them my own
mistakes and all worth naming:

  - the first mutation changed only the fallback, which the chain read
    immediately overwrites, so it tested nothing;
  - the second broke the build, and `npm run build >/dev/null 2>&1` hid
    that while http-server happily served the previous dist — everything
    "passed" against a bundle that no longer existed in source;
  - the check itself read the diamond from inside the PAGE, where CORS
    made it return null, and `!live ||` then passed. It reads from node
    now, and a failed read is a failed check.

Put the old address back with the chain read removed and it fails with
"diamond says 0x3085c895…, panel shows 0x20d9CcAA…".

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

settled on Coston2 — delivery versus payment, in one transaction

  0x09f55efa91c30ce3224d2235b98864126cb0481136496cbc072414940c502612

relayClearing verified the enclave's signature and the set digest, moved the
clearing price from the winner to the maker and the lot to the winner, and
closed the auction. RFQ 2 on 0x3085C895…D702: winner 0x428837B1…0762,
clearing price 0.5 FXRP — the reserve, which is what a lone bid pays.

Until today this could not happen at all. Getting there needed four things,
and only the first was known when I started.

The enclave emitted JSON while the contract rebuilds abi.encode(rfqId,
winner, clearingPrice, setDigest) and hashes THAT — so no clearing this
system ever produced was verifiable on-chain. Fixed in processClearAuction,
with a test that fails on 180 bytes where 128 are required.

teeAddress was wrong in every deployment. The original was the deployer's
own address. My second attempt used an address I recovered with the broken
layout, which is a different wrong address per message — I should have
recovered from a second clearing before trusting the first, and that check
took ten seconds once I thought to run it. setTeeAddress is one-shot, so
each mistake cost a redeploy. Extension 65642 is ours, and
setExtensionContracts rebinds it, so redeploying is cheap.

Restarting extension-tee mints a new machine key, which I documented weeks
ago and then walked into anyway: the rebuild for the encoding fix invalidated
the registration mid-run. Re-registered, old machine retired, active set back
to one.

And FXRP refuses a self-transfer. relayClearing moves the price from the
winner to the maker, so a demo where one wallet plays both roles reverts
CannotTransferToSelf() no matter what else is right. scripts/onchain-loop.ts
uses a real counterparty now, and runs the whole thing end to end.

SUBMISSION.md carries the settlement, and verify:submission checks it against
the chain along with the other eight claims.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

relayClearing could never have verified a real clearing

Running the whole thing on Coston2 — post, seal, request, settle — found it.
relayClearing reverted BadTeeSignature on a clearing that was honest, whose
set digest matched the contract's own byte for byte.

The node signs the result data AS IT IS. The contract never receives those
bytes: it rebuilds them with abi.encode(rfqId, winner, clearingPrice,
setDigest) and hashes that. The enclave emitted JSON. The two could not
agree, so no clearing this system produced was ever verifiable on-chain.

The Foundry test did not catch it because it signs the abi-encoded form
itself — it was checking the contract against its own assumption rather
than against the enclave. "Settlement proven on a fork" was proven against
a copy that shared the mistake.

processClearAuction now emits exactly what relayClearing rebuilds. Going
back to json.Marshal fails the new test with "the clearing returned 180
bytes, not the 128 the contract rebuilds".

Two things this cost on the way, both worth recording:

The desk's mirror of that check in lib/verify.ts was wrong in the same way,
and I trusted it. It recovered 0x84486df4… from one clearing, I took that
for the enclave's address, and burned the one-shot setTeeAddress on it.
Recovering from a SECOND clearing gave a different address — which is what a
wrong layout does, and the check I should have run first. With the right
layout both clearings recover to 0x175fb864…A9A7, exactly the registered TEE
machine id.

So the deployed contract's teeAddress was wrong twice over: the original was
the DEPLOYER's own address, and setTeeAddress reverts TeeAlreadySet after
the first call. Both deployments are permanently unable to settle. Extension
65642 is ours (getExtensionOwner), and setExtensionContracts can rebind it,
so this is fixable with a redeploy rather than a new registration.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitBid and relayClearing, from the desk

The two ends of the on-chain path that were never wired, so the chain of
custody the design rests on had a gap in the middle and another at the end.

commitBid. The direct rail records a commitment in enclave memory; only a
transaction puts it in the set the CONTRACT keeps, and that set is what
relayClearing checks a clearing against. A commitment that never reached
the chain can demonstrate the mechanism but can never be part of a
settlement. Both rails now build the same sealed envelope through one
sealBidEnvelope() — a commitment computed differently on one of them would
be refused by the enclave with nothing pointing at why.

relayClearing is the only function that moves money, and it had never been
called from anywhere. It settles delivery versus payment in one
transaction: the winner pays the maker the second price, the lot moves to
the winner. It refuses a clearing whose signature does not recover to the
registered enclave, and one whose setDigest is not the digest of the
commitments it recorded — so an auctioneer who dropped an inconvenient bid
produces a settlement that reverts rather than a price nobody can question.

Both check what the contract checks before the wallet is asked to sign:
four revert conditions for a bid, four for a settlement, all of them
public reads. Ten tests, and removing the set-digest comparison — the
check the whole security argument rests on — fails one.

The desk also says plainly when a clearing cannot be settled: the dev
facade signs nothing, and relayClearing will not take an unsigned outcome.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

the sealed reserve rides the transaction, and the pair with it

postRfq takes `bytes encryptedReserve` and the on-chain rail was sending
`0x`. That cost more than the floor: the PAIR travels in the same
envelope, so an on-chain block was recorded with no reserve AND no pair
name at all. A zero floor is the giveaway the post form already refuses on
the other rail — this was the same giveaway by a different route.

sealReserve() encrypts {reserve, pair} to the enclave's key, from the
chain, the same path a bid takes.

The test for it was inert on its first outing, which is the fourth time
that has happened and worth writing down. It built a ciphertext, posted
PLAINTEXT over the direct rail, and asserted the plaintext survived — the
envelope was never opened by anyone, and deleting the encryption entirely
would not have failed it. Only decodePostRfq calls the Decryptor, so it
now goes through the extension's instruction endpoint, which is the path
that actually decrypts. Sending `0x` — exactly what the desk used to send
— fails it with "the pair rides in the sealed envelope and must survive
the round trip".

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

a zero reserve gave the lot away, and a receipt did not say who vouched for it

Clearing floors AT the reserve, so a block posted with the reserve field
left empty means a single bid takes the lot for nothing. The field was
optional and said nothing about that; a live clearing came back "winner
0x7099… at 0" and that is what it was. Refused now, with the reason.

And the receipt said "Vickrey second price" with no indication of who
stood behind the number. The contract checks the enclave's signature
before it settles — relayClearing recovers the signer against the
registered teeAddress and rejects anything that does not — but the direct
rail's facade signs nothing at all, which is worth reading rather than
discovering. lib/verify.ts mirrors that check for the desk to make itself,
and reports "the operator's word" for exactly the case where it is.

The escape hatch is the honest part of the key fix. cmd/dev generates its
own key and registers nothing, so encrypting to the registered key against
a local enclave produces "ecies: invalid message" and nothing else —
reading the key from the chain broke local development outright.
VITE_ALLOW_UNVERIFIED_TEE_KEY exists for that, off by default, and the bid
form says out loud when it is on: "UNVERIFIED KEY: this build encrypts to
whatever the relay serves, so the relay can read your bid."

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

the desk asked the operator for the key that hides bids from the operator

A bid opening is ECIES-encrypted so that only the enclave can read it, and
teePublicKey() fetched that key from the operator's own GET /info. An
